'''''Echinacea purpurea''''', the '''eastern purple coneflower''',<ref name=b/> '''purple coneflower''', '''hedgehog coneflower''', or '''Echinacea''', is a [[North America]]n [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]].<ref name=Zimmerman>{{Cite web |url=http://www.brucezimmerman.com/ARTICLES/ECHINACEA.htm |first=Bruce |last=Zimmerman |work=Gardening |name-list-style=vanc |title=Echinacea: Not always a purple coneflower. |access-date=2009-08-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304083546/http://www.brucezimmerman.com/ARTICLES/ECHINACEA.htm |archive-date=2016-03-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is [[native plant|native]] to parts of eastern North America and present to some extent in the wild in much of the [[Eastern United States|eastern]], [[Southeastern United States|southeastern]] and [[midwestern United States]], as well as in the Canadian Province of [[Ontario]]. It is most common in the [[Ozarks]], the [[Mississippi Valley]], and the [[Ohio Valley]]. Its [[habitat]]s include dry open woods, prairies, and barrens.

==Description==
''Echinacea purpurea'' is an [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[Perennial plant|perennial]] up to {{convert|120|cm|in|0|abbr=off|sp=us}} tall by {{convert|25|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} wide at maturity. Depending on the climate, it blooms throughout summer into autumn. Its cone-shaped [[flowering heads]] are usually, but not always, purple in the wild. Its individual flowers (florets) within the [[flower head]] are [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]], having both male and female organs in each flower. It is [[Pollination|pollinated]] by butterflies and bees. The alternate leaves, borne by a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] from {{convert|0 to 17|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}, are oval to [[lanceolate]], {{convert|5-30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|5-12|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} wide; the margin is tightened to toothed.

The [[inflorescence]] is a [[Capitulum (flower)|capitulum]], {{convert|7 to 15|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} in diameter, formed by a prominent domed central protuberance consisting of multiple small yellow florets. These are surrounded by a ring of pink or purple [[ligulate]] florets. The tubular florets are [[hermaphrodite]] while the ligular florets are [[Sterility (physiology)|sterile]]. The [[Bract#Involucral bracts|involucral bracts]] are linear to [[lanceolate]]. The plant prefers well-drained soils in full sun.<ref name=b>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220004561 |work=Flora of North America |title=Eastern purple coneflower, ''Echinacea purpurea'' (Linnaeus) Moench, Methodus. 591. 1794.}}</ref> The fruit is an [[achene]], sought after by birds.

==Taxonomy==
''Echinacea'' is derived from [[Greek language|Greek]], meaning 'spiny one', in reference to the spiny [[Sea urchin|sea urchins]] 'εχίνοι' which the ripe flower heads of species of this genus resemble. The epithet ''purpurea'' means 'reddish-purple'.<ref name="gledhill">{{cite book |last=Gledhill |first=David |name-list-style=vanc |date=2008 |title=The Names of Plants |url=https://archive.org/details/namesplants00gled_746 |url-access=limited |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=9780521866453 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/namesplants00gled_746/page/n158 149], 321 }}</ref>

The species was named ''Rudbeckia purpurea'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.<ref>{{cite book| author=Linnaeus, C.| title=Species plantarum| date=1753| page=907| url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/26068878}}</ref> Linnaeus took the placement in the genus ''Rudbeckia'' from [[Jan Frederik Gronovius]].<ref>{{cite book| author=Gronovius, J.F.| title=Flora virginica| date=1743| page=104| url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/48313105}}</ref> He and Linnaeus based the name on a description under the name "Chrysanthemum americanum" given by [[Leonard Plukenet]], published in 1696.<ref>{{cite book| author=Plukenet, L.| title=Almagestum botanicum| date=1696| page=99| url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/10874/?offset=#page=103&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=}}</ref> In 1794, [[Conrad Moench]] placed it in genus ''[[Echinacea]]'' as ''Echinacea purpurea''.<ref name=HeKaarlas/>

In 1818, [[Thomas Nuttall]] described what he thought to be a variety and named it ''Rudbeckia purpurea'' var. ''serotina''.<ref>{{Cite book| last=Nuttall| first=Th.| year=1818| title=The genera of North American plants| volume=2| pages=178| url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/723931}}</ref> In 1823, [[Robert Sweet (botanist)|Robert Sweet]] raised this variety to the rank of species as ''Rudbeckia serotina''.<ref>{{Cite book| last=Sweet| first=R.| title=The British flower garden| year=1823| volume=1| page=t.4| url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/53208027}}</ref> In 1832, [[George Don]] moved it to the genus ''Echinacea'' as ''Echinacea serotina''.<ref name=HeKaarlas>{{cite book | last1=He| first1=Y.| last2=Kaarlas| first2=M.| chapter=Popularity, Diversity and Quality of Echinacea| editor-last1=Miller| editor-first1=S.C.| editor-last2=Yu| editor-first2=H.| title=Echinacea: The genus Echinacea| publisher=CRC Press| date=2004 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book| last=Don| first=G.| editor-last=Loudon| editor-first=J.C.| editor-link=John Claudius Loudon| title=Loudon's hortus britannicus| edition=2nd| pages=587| url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/46026179}}</ref> In 2001, Shannon Binns et al. discovered a misapplication of the name ''Echinacea purpurea'' {{small|(L.) Moench}} for the taxon correctly named ''Echinacea serotina'' {{small|(Nutt.) G.Don}} in 1832. The authors proposed to conserve the name with a conserved [[Type (biology)|type]] so as not to change a long standing name which would have caused confusion among gardeners and herbalists.<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Binns| first1=S.E.| last2=Baum| first2=B.R.| last3=Arnason| first3=J.T.| title=Proposal to conserve the name ''Rudbeckia purpurea'' L. (Asteraceae) with a conserved type| date=2001| journal=Taxon| volume=50| issue=4| page=1199–1200| doi=10.2307/1224745}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last1=Binns| first1=S.E.| last2=Arnason| first2=J.T. | last3=Baum| first3=B.R.| editor-last1=Miller| editor-first1=S.C.| editor-last2=Yu| editor-first2=H.| chapter=Taxonomic history and revision of the genus ''Echinacea''| title=Echinacea: The genus Echinacea |publisher=CRC Press |date=2004 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Echinacea purpurea'' is [[native plant|native]] to parts of eastern North America{{r|pfaf}} and present to some extent in the wild in much of the eastern, southeastern and midwestern United States as well as in the Canadian Province of [[Ontario]]. It is most common in the [[Ozarks]], the [[Mississippi Valley]], and the [[Ohio Valley]].<ref name="PLANTS">{{Cite PLANTS |taxon=Echinacea purpurea | symbol=ECPU |access-date=10 December 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{BONAP |genus=Echinacea |species=purpurea |date=2014 |access-date=10 December 2024}}</ref> Its [[habitat]]s include dry open woods, [[prairies]], and barrens.

==Cultivation==
[[File:Echinacea purpurea.JPG|thumb|Plants raised outdoors]]
''Echinacea purpurea'' is grown as an [[ornamental plant]] in temperate regions. It is ideal for curbs, walkways, or beds. The flowers can also go into the composition of fresh bouquets. Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been developed for flower quality and plant form.<ref name=Zimmerman/> The plant grows in sun or light shade.{{r|midgely1999}} It thrives in either dry or moist soil and can tolerate drought once established. The cultivars 'Ruby Giant'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Echinacea purpurea'' 'Ruby Giant'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/175792/Echinacea-purpurea-Ruby-Giant/Details | access-date = 4 June 2020}}</ref> and 'Elbrook'<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/179552/Echinacea-purpurea-Elton-Knight-Elbrook-(PBR)/Details|title=RHS Plantfinder - ''Echinacea'' 'Elbrook' |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf |title=AGM Plants - Ornamental |date=July 2017 |page=33 |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |access-date=6 February 2018}}</ref>

===Propagation===
''Echinacea purpurea'' is [[plant propagation|propagated]] either [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] or from [[seed]]s.{{r|pfaf}} Useful vegetative techniques include division, root cuttings, and basal cuttings. Clumps can be [[division (horticulture)|divided]], or broken into smaller bunches, which is normally done in the spring or autumn. Cuttings made from roots that are "pencil-sized" will develop into plants when started in late autumn or early winter.<ref name=Zimmerman/> Cuttings of basal shoots in the spring may be rooted when treated with [[Auxin#Root growth and development|rooting hormones]], such as IBA at 1000 ppm.<ref name="Plant Delights">{{cite web|last1=Carey|first1=Dennis|last2=Avent|first2=Tony|name-list-style=vanc |title=Echinacea Explosion - The Purple Coneflower Chronicles|url=http://www.plantdelights.com/Article/Echinacea-Coneflower|website=Plant Delights Nursery Article|publisher=Plant Delights Nursery|access-date=2015-07-12}}</ref>

Seed [[germination]] occurs best with daily temperature fluctuations{{r|pfaf}} or after stratification,<ref name="PLANTS"/> which help to end [[Dormancy#Dormant seeds|dormancy]]. Seeds may be started indoors in advance of the growing season or outdoors after the growing season has started.

==Ecology==
Many pollinators are attracted to ''E. purpurea''. Bees that are attracted to the flowers include [[bumblebees]], [[Halictidae|sweat bees]], [[honey bees]], the [[Megachile pugnata|sunflower leafcutter bee]], and the mining bee ''Andrena helianthiformis''. Butterflies that visit include [[monarch butterfly|monarchs]], [[swallowtail butterflies]], and [[sulphur butterflies]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=The Xerxes Society |title=100 Plants to Feed the Bees |date=2016 |publisher=Storey Publishing |isbn=978-1-61212-886-3 |pages=87}}</ref> Birds, particularly [[finches]], eat the seeds and disperse them through their droppings.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Echinacea purpurea'' |url=http://bioweb.uwlax.edu/bio203/2011/stiefel_bran/interactions.htm |website=bioweb.uwlax.edu}}</ref>

[[Slug]]s{{r|pfaf}} and [[rabbit]]s will also eat the foliage when young, or shortly after emerging in the spring.<ref>{{cite web |title=Echinacea – How To Grow Purple Coneflower |url=https://growitbuildit.com/2018/09/16/echinacea-how-to-grow-purple-coneflower/ |website=Growit Buildit |access-date=25 September 2018 |date=2018-09-16 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Additionally, roots can be damaged and eaten by [[gopher]]s.<ref name="PLANTS" />

==Chemistry==
''Echinacea purpurea'' contains alkamides, [[caffeic acid]] derivatives, [[polysaccharide]]s, and [[glycoprotein]]s.<ref name="Saeidnia 2015 63">{{cite journal |vauthors=Manayi A, Vazirian M, Saeidnia S |title=''Echinacea purpurea'': Pharmacology, phytochemistry and analysis methods |journal=Pharmacognosy Reviews |volume=9 |issue=17 |pages=63–72 |date=2015 |pmid=26009695 |pmc=4441164 |doi=10.4103/0973-7847.156353 |doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Nicotiflorin]] is the dominant [[flavonoid]] in ''E. purpurea'', followed by the flavonoid [[rutin]].<ref name="Kurkin 905–906">{{Cite journal|last1=Kurkin|first1=V. A.|last2=Akushskaya|first2=A. S.|last3=Avdeeva|first3=E. V.|last4=Velmyaikina|first4=E. I.|last5=Daeva|first5=E. D.|last6=Kadentsev|first6=V. I.|date=2011-12-01|title=Flavonoids from ''Echinacea purpurea''|journal=Russian Journal of Bioorganic Chemistry|language=en|volume=37|issue=7|pages=905–906|doi=10.1134/S1068162011070120|s2cid=30930227|issn=1608-330X}}</ref>

==Traditional medicine==
{{Further|Echinacea#Uses{{!}}Uses of ''Echinacea''}}

[[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] have used the plant as [[traditional medicine]] to treat many ailments.<ref name="drugs">{{cite web |title=Echinacea |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/echinacea.html |website=Drugs.com |access-date=16 September 2021 |date=8 April 2021}}</ref>
